title: Optics and Telescopes
intro: Telescopes are giant eyes, and almost everything we know about the universe beyond our solar system arrives as light. Follow the light from the eye and the camera (refraction, focus, focal plane, exposure, pixels) to the two key properties of a telescope: light-collecting area, which grows with the diameter squared, and angular resolution, limited by diffraction in proportion to wavelength divided by diameter. Then see why research telescopes are reflectors, what imaging, spectroscopy and time monitoring can and cannot measure, how the atmosphere blurs, brightens and blocks light, what adaptive optics and space telescopes fix, how each kind of invisible light is observed, how interferometry links telescopes for sharper detail, and how neutrinos, cosmic rays and gravitational waves carry information that is not light at all.

learningObjectives.text: Compare how the eye and a camera form images, including the roles of the lens, the retina or detector and the image plane.
Explain how telescope aperture affects light collection and how telescope design affects image sharpness.
Identify the properties of astronomical objects that can be measured from their light.
Explain how Earth's atmosphere affects observations and compare observing sites.
Compare what astronomers can learn from spectra and from non-visible astronomical messengers.
Compare the light-collecting power of two telescopes using the rule that area is proportional to diameter squared.
Predict how angular resolution changes when the mirror diameter or the wavelength changes (it is proportional to wavelength divided by diameter), and say how interferometry helps.
Explain why most large research telescopes are reflectors rather than refractors, and describe where the focus is in the main reflector designs.
Choose imaging, spectroscopy or time monitoring for a given astronomical question and say what each one measures.
Match each kind of light, from radio waves to gamma rays, with a suitable telescope design and a ground or space location.

sections.title: How light bends: refraction, lenses and mirrors

img.alt: Three photos of refraction: a light beam shifting sideways through a glass block, a pen that looks bent in a bowl of water, and cars on a road with a shiny wet-looking surface.

steps.title: Refraction: light changes direction
bullets: **Refraction** is the bending of light as it passes from one material into another, for example from air into glass, water or the eye. Lenses, including the lens in your eye, focus light by refraction.

Why it bends: light travels more slowly in denser material. When a wave meets glass at a slant, the part of each wave crest that reaches the glass first slows down first, the rest of the crest swings round, and the beam turns.
A little of the light does not go in at all: it bounces off the surface (reflection), leaving at the same angle it arrived.
Everyday refraction: a beam shifted sideways by a glass block, a pen that looks broken where it enters water, a road that looks wet on a hot day.
Air refracts too. The setting Sun looks squashed because light from its lower edge crosses more air and is bent slightly more than light from its upper edge.

img.alt: A lens bending parallel red, green and blue rays so that blue crosses the axis nearest the lens and red farthest away, labelled chromatic aberration.

steps.title: Lenses split colours: chromatic aberration
bullets: How strongly glass bends light depends a little on the wavelength: blue light is bent more than red light.

So a simple lens brings each colour to a focus at a slightly different distance, blue nearest the lens and red farthest. This is **chromatic aberration**, and it shows up as coloured fringes around bright objects.
Combining lenses made of different kinds of glass reduces the problem, but it is a built-in weakness of lenses.
A mirror reflects every colour at the same angle, so mirrors have no chromatic aberration, which is one reason big telescopes use them.

img.alt: Parallel light rays reflecting off a concave mirror and meeting at a focal point on the same side as the incoming light, with the focal length marked.

steps.title: Mirrors focus by reflection
bullets: A **concave** mirror (curved inward, like the inside of a bowl) also brings parallel rays to a focus, but by reflection instead of refraction.
Its focus lies in front of the mirror, on the same side as the incoming light; a lens focuses light on the far side.
The **focal length** is the distance from the mirror (or lens) to the point where parallel rays meet.
Light never travels through a mirror, so only its front surface has to be shaped precisely. That makes very large mirrors far easier to build and support than very large lenses.

boxes.text: Why does slowing down make light turn? Picture a row of people walking arm in arm from pavement onto sand at a slant. Those who step onto the sand first slow down, so the whole row pivots. The crests of a light wave do the same at the edge of a piece of glass.
Three look-alike words: reFRACTion = light bends going through (lenses). reFLECTion = light bounces back (mirrors). DIFFraction = waves spreading and interfering (it limits sharpness).
A lens forms an image by refraction, not by reflection, transmission, absorption or diffraction. Chromatic aberration is a lens problem only; mirrors do not have it (Ch6.1 slide 8).

sections.title: Forming an image: the focus and the focal plane

img.alt: A tree lit by the Sun with rays running from two points on the tree to a plain screen, labelled as giving no image, only a blurry mess of scattered light.

steps.title: A bare screen shows no image
bullets: Every point of a sunlit tree scatters light in all directions, so every spot on a plain screen receives light from every part of the tree.
All that light piles up into an even, blurry glow. To make an image, each spot must receive light from just one point of the object: something has to sort the rays.

img.alt: A tree lit by the Sun, with rays passing through a tiny hole in a box to form a small flipped copy of the tree on the back wall.

steps.title: A pinhole sorts the rays
bullets: A tiny hole lets through only one narrow ray from each point of the object, so each point lands on its own spot and an image appears.
The rays cross at the hole, so the image is flipped top to bottom and left to right.
The catch: so little light gets through that the image is very dim. Widen the hole and it gets brighter but blurrier.

img.alt: Parallel light rays from a distant object passing through a convex lens and meeting at the focal point on the focal plane, with the focal length marked.

steps.title: A lens brings parallel rays to a focus
bullets: A lens sorts rays far better than a pinhole: it accepts a wide beam and bends it. Rays that hit far from the centre are bent the most, and a ray through the very centre is not bent.
Light from a very distant object, such as a star, arrives as **parallel rays**. The lens bends them so they meet at one point, the **focus** (or **focal point**).
This is why distant stars look like points of light to our eyes and in photographs.
To see or record the image a lens or telescope makes, the eye or the detector must be placed at the focus.

img.alt: Rays from the top and bottom of a tree crossing at a convex lens and forming an upside-down tree at the image plane.

steps.title: The image forms on the focal plane
bullets: Rays from different parts of an object come from different directions. The lens bends the light from each point of the object to its own point, and together these points make an image.
The surface where the image is sharp is the **focal plane** (also called the image plane). Its exact position depends on the object's distance and the lens's focal length.
The image made by a single lens is **upside down**. Your eyes form upside-down images too, and your brain turns them the right way up.
A detector placed in front of or behind the focal plane records a blurred picture.

boxes.text: Focusing is sorting: the lens sends all the light that comes from one direction to one spot. A distant star is a single direction, so it becomes a single point on the focal plane.
Parallel in, point out: parallel rays from a star meet at the focus, and the eye or detector goes on the focal plane.

If you are asked where to put your eye to see the image a telescope forms, the answer is the focus, not the primary mirror, the secondary mirror or the hole in the primary. 'Cassegrain' is the name of a design, not a place. The pinhole steps come from Ch6.1 slides 2-3.

sections.title: Eyes and cameras: our everyday light sensors

steps.title: How the eye works
bullets: Almost everything we know about the universe beyond our solar system arrives as light, and telescopes work like giant eyes, so the eye is the place to start.
**Pupil**: the opening that sets how much light gets in. It widens (dilates) in dim light and narrows in bright light; the coloured iris around it does the adjusting.

**Lens** (helped by the clear cornea in front of it): bends the incoming light by refraction so that it comes to a focus on the retina. Focusing is its job; it does not control the amount of light or send signals.
**Retina**: the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. Its cells (rods and cones) fire when light reaches them and send signals to the brain through the optic nerve.

steps.title: The retina is the eye's focal plane
bullets: A glass lens and the eye do the same thing: both bend parallel rays to a focus.
When an eye focuses perfectly, its focal plane lands right on the retina and the picture there is sharp. (The retina is actually curved, but we can treat it as the image plane.)
As with any single lens, the image on the retina is upside down, and the brain flips it.

steps.title: A camera is an eye that keeps the picture
bullets: A camera copies the eye: a small opening lets light in (like the pupil), a lens focuses it, and a **detector** (image sensor) on the focal plane records it, where the retina would be. Old cameras used film; today's detectors are electronic.
The **shutter** works like an eyelid: light reaches the detector only while it is open.
The **exposure time** is how long light is allowed to collect. A longer exposure lets more total light pile up, so details too faint for a short exposure appear. It does not make the image sharper.
The trade-off: long exposures can leave bright regions **overexposed**, meaning so many photons pile up there that the detector cannot count them accurately anymore.

img.alt: A diagram of a CCD in which green photons strike a grid of pixels and release electrons, which are read out row by row through an amplifier to a digital converter.

steps.title: Pixels count photons
bullets: Electronic detectors such as **CCDs** (charge-coupled devices) are chips divided into a grid of **pixels** (picture elements).

Each photon that strikes a pixel adds a little electric charge. After the exposure a computer measures the charge in every pixel, which tells how many photons hit it, and the picture is stored as an array of numbers.
Consumer cameras now have 10 million or more pixels; telescope cameras join many large CCDs, each with millions of pixels.
Modern detectors record a far wider range of brightness, much more accurately, than photographic film did.

steps.title: Better detectors and image processing
bullets: Detectors keep improving, and that pays off directly: fitting a modern detector to an old telescope can greatly increase what it can do.
Spectra of distant galaxies used to take huge effort one at a time; detectors that record hundreds or thousands of spectra at once now make it routine.
**Image processing**: most pictures you see have been combined and adjusted after they were taken, for example sharpened, colour-balanced, corrected for over- or underexposure, or cleaned of defects.
Used carefully, processing brings out real details that would stay hidden; misused, it can distort what the camera actually recorded.

boxes.text: A detector is a photon counter. Leaving the shutter open longer, or using a bigger opening, puts more photons into every pixel, so faint objects finally stand out.
Pupil = how MUCH light, lens = WHERE it focuses, retina = RECORDS it. A camera has the same three jobs, plus a shutter for an eyelid.

The lens of the eye bends light so it focuses on the retina; adjusting the amount of light is the pupil's job, and sending signals is the retina and optic nerve. The benefit of a longer exposure is more total light, not better angular resolution, faster timing or shorter wavelengths.

sections.title: Key property 1: light-collecting area

img.alt: Two ray diagrams with photos of a twig bud: a wide lens gives a bright image with a blurred background, and a narrow lens gives a dimmer image with more of the scene in focus.

steps.title: A wider opening gathers more light
bullets: Telescopes are giant eyes whose main advantage is that they collect far more light than a pupil can. Their two most important properties are **light-collecting area** (how much light) and **angular resolution** (how fine the detail).

Light-collecting area means how much light a telescope gathers at once. Because telescopes are round, we label them by the width of the main mirror or lens, called the **aperture**: a '10-meter telescope' is one whose collecting surface measures 10 m across.
More area means more light every second, so a brighter image in less exposure time, and fainter objects come within reach.

The photos show a side effect seen in camera lenses: a wide lens gives more light but a shallower **depth of field** (less of the scene in focus at once); a narrow one gives less light but more of the scene in focus.

steps.title: Area grows with the diameter squared
bullets: The area of a circle is proportional to its diameter squared (A = πD²/4), so the light collected is proportional to **D²**. A small increase in diameter gives a big increase in light.
Double the diameter and the light goes up 2² = **4 times**. A 10 m telescope collects 4 times as much as a 5 m telescope, not 2 times.
A 10 m telescope has 5 times the diameter of a 2 m telescope, so it collects 5² = 25 times as much light.
A 10 m mirror is more than 1000 times as wide as your pupil, so it gathers more light than 1000² = a million human eyes.
Area and exposure time trade off: with 4 times the area you collect the same light in a quarter of the time.

img.alt: An artist's picture of the 39.3 m Extremely Large Telescope dome, the four-telescope Very Large Telescope and the Colosseum side by side for scale.

steps.title: How big are the biggest telescopes?
bullets: Today's largest visible-light telescopes are about 10 m across, for example the Gran Telescopio Canarias (10.4 m), the twin Keck telescopes (10 m each) and the four 8.2 m units of the Very Large Telescope in Chile.
For more than 40 years before the 1990s, the 5 m Hale telescope on Mount Palomar was the most powerful in the world; it is no longer even in the top ten.

Three giants are planned. The **Extremely Large Telescope** in Chile's Atacama Desert, already under construction, will combine 798 mirror segments into a 39.3 m mirror, about (39.3/10)² ≈ 15 times the light of a Keck telescope.

The Giant Magellan Telescope (Chile) will use seven 8.4 m mirrors that act like one 21 m mirror. The Thirty Meter Telescope has been held up by controversy over building on Maunakea, a mountain of great importance in Hawaiian culture.

boxes.text: A mirror catches light over its whole surface, like a bucket catching rain. A bucket twice as wide has an opening four times as large, so it catches four times the rain in the same time.
Ratio, then square: (big diameter ÷ small diameter)² = how many times more light.

Light collected goes with the diameter SQUARED; sharpness goes only with the diameter. 10 m versus 5 m: 4 times the light but only 2 times the sharpness. Dates differ between sources: Ch6.2 pt1 slide 3 says 30+ m telescopes will work in the 2030s, while the 2022 printing scheduled the ELT for 2027.

sections.title: Key property 2: angular resolution (and why magnification is not the point)

img.alt: An illustration of a car's headlights and a distant light on a road, with the angle between two lights as seen by a person marked as the angular separation.

steps.title: Telling two points apart
bullets: **Angular resolution** is the smallest angle by which two points of light, such as two stars, can be separated and still be seen as two. A smaller angle means finer detail.

The **angular separation** of two objects depends on how far apart they really are and on how far away they are. A car's headlights look well apart when the car is close, then blend into one as it drives away.

If two stars are closer together in the sky than the telescope's angular resolution, you see one blurred point of light: not two points, and not nothing. Stars 0.1 arcsecond apart seen with 0.6 arcsecond resolution make one spot.

Scale: 1 degree = 60 arcminutes and 1 arcminute = 60 arcseconds. The human eye resolves about 1 arcminute; the 2.4 m Hubble Space Telescope about 0.05 arcsecond in visible light, sharp enough to read ordinary print from almost 1 km away.

img.alt: Colourful overlapping circular ripples from two sources, showing how waves interfere where they meet.

steps.title: Diffraction sets the limit
bullets: Light is a wave, and overlapping waves **interfere**, like two sets of ripples on a pond: where crest meets crest the water rises extra high, where crest meets trough the surface goes flat.
Inside a telescope this interference, called **diffraction**, spreads every point of light a little. So even a perfect telescope in space has a best possible resolution, its **diffraction limit**.

The limit depends on mirror diameter D and wavelength λ: smallest angle ∝ **λ/D**. At a given wavelength a bigger telescope has a smaller (better) limit; with a given telescope, longer wavelengths give a larger (worse) limit.

Double the diameter and the smallest angle halves, so a 10 m telescope resolves details half the size of those a 5 m telescope can (a factor of 2, not 4). Double the wavelength and the smallest angle doubles.
That is why, to see detail as fine as a visible-light telescope does, a radio telescope has to be far bigger.

img.alt: A Hubble Space Telescope image of a single star showing a bright centre surrounded by faint rings and a blotchy halo.

steps.title: A star is never a perfect point
bullets: Look closely at a Hubble image of a single star: a bright core surrounded by rings and blotches. This pattern made from one point of light is the **point-spread function**, and it comes from diffraction.
With better angular resolution (a bigger mirror or a shorter wavelength) the rings would be smaller. Good optics keep the pattern small, but it can never be removed.

On the ground, moving air usually blurs images to about 0.5 arcsecond, far worse than a large telescope's diffraction limit, so most ground telescopes never reach their theoretical sharpness without help.

steps.title: Magnification is not the key property
bullets: Many people assume that magnifying power is what matters most in a telescope. It is not.
Enlarging an image cannot reveal details smaller than the angular resolution, or objects too faint for the light collected. Too much magnification just gives a bigger blur.

Choosing a telescope of your own: look at the aperture (light-collecting area), the optical quality and how portable it is. A telescope advertised only by its power, such as '650 power', is rarely a good one.
Binoculars are labelled like 7 × 35: 7 is the magnification and 35 is the diameter of each lens in millimetres. Bigger lenses give more light but are heavier to hold steady.
A small telescope will not show the views in professional photographs, which come from large telescopes and long exposures, and even a computer-guided one needs setting up before each use.

boxes.text: A wave squeezed through an opening spreads out, and the narrower the opening compared with the wavelength, the more it spreads. A wide mirror lets the wave blur less, and shorter waves blur less through any opening.
Smallest angle ∝ λ/D: to see finer detail, go wider (bigger D) or go bluer (smaller λ). Small angle = sharp image.

Resolution improves by the ratio of the diameters (10 m versus 5 m: 2 times better), while light improves by the square (4 times). A better resolution is a SMALLER number. Stars closer than the resolution appear as one blurred point. The diffraction limit limits angular resolution, not size or spectral resolution.

sections.title: The two basic designs: refracting and reflecting telescopes

img.alt: Two ray diagrams: a lens focusing parallel rays for a refracting telescope and a curved mirror focusing them for a reflecting telescope.

steps.title: Two ways to focus starlight
bullets: A **refracting telescope** collects and focuses light with a large glass lens, just as an eye does. The earliest telescopes, including Galileo's, were refractors.

In a **reflecting telescope**, light is gathered by a carefully curved **primary mirror**. It bounces the light up to a smaller **secondary mirror**, and that mirror passes it to a focus where an eye or an instrument can use it.
The secondary mirror sits in the path of the incoming light, but it blocks only a small fraction, so in practice this is no problem.

img.alt: A large refracting telescope inside an observatory dome beside a drawing of the lens at the top of the tube, with starlight passing down to the eyepiece and focus.

steps.title: Why big refractors lost out
bullets: The largest refractor ever built, at Yerkes Observatory (finished 1897), has a lens 1 m across and a tube 19.5 m long.
Reason 1: light goes through a lens, so the whole lens must be clear, flawless glass with both faces precisely shaped. A mirror needs only its reflecting surface to be precise.

Reason 2: big lenses are very heavy and can be held only by their edges, at the top of the tube, where they are hard to steady and tend to sag. A primary mirror sits at the bottom and can be supported across its whole back.
Lenses also absorb some infrared and ultraviolet light and suffer chromatic aberration. So nearly all research telescopes today are reflectors.

img.alt: A large refracting telescope inside an observatory dome beside a drawing of the lens at the top of the tube, with starlight passing down to the eyepiece and focus.

steps.title: Where the focus is: Cassegrain, Newtonian, Nasmyth
bullets: **Cassegrain focus**: the secondary sends the light back down through a hole in the centre of the primary to cameras and instruments underneath. The 8 m Gemini North telescope on Maunakea works this way.
**Newtonian focus**: the secondary sends the light out through the side of the tube near the top.
**Nasmyth or Coudé focus**: a third mirror sends the light out the side lower down, where large, heavy instruments can sit.
Whatever the design, the eye or detector goes at the focus; the names only say where that focus is.

img.alt: Two photos: the segmented mirror of the Keck II telescope and the gold hexagonal mirror of the James Webb Space Telescope with two people in clean suits for scale.

steps.title: Lighter and segmented mirrors
bullets: For a long time the sheer weight of glass limited how big a reflector could be.
Two inventions removed that limit: lighter single mirrors (such as Gemini's 8 m mirror) and **segmented mirrors**, many small mirrors that work together as one large one.
Each 10 m Keck telescope's mirror is a honeycomb of 36 hexagons. JWST's 6.5 m mirror has 18 gold-coated hexagons, folded to fit inside its rocket. The Extremely Large Telescope will use 798.
These mirror technologies are behind today's boom in very large telescopes.

boxes.text: A lens works by light passing through it, so it must be perfect inside and can be held only by its rim. A mirror works only at its surface, so it can be braced from behind or built from tiles.
Refractor: heavy lens on TOP (sags, long tube, colour fringes). Reflector: mirror at the BOTTOM (supported, can be segmented, no colour fringes).

The good reason for reflectors is that the heaviest part (the mirror) sits at the bottom where it can be supported, and only its surface must be perfect. It is NOT that a mirror of the same diameter collects more light (same area, same light), and not that reflectors are taller or smaller.

sections.title: What astronomers do with telescopes: imaging

img.alt: Three separate images of the Trifid Nebula taken through blue, green and red filters, joined to a full colour combined image.

steps.title: Three kinds of observation, starting with imaging
bullets: Most observations fall into three categories: **imaging** (taking pictures), **spectroscopy** (spreading light into spectra) and **time monitoring** (tracking how something changes).
An imaging instrument is basically a camera. Astronomers often put a **filter** in front of it so that only one colour, or band of wavelengths, gets through.
The detector only counts light, so the rich colour pictures you see are made by combining separate images taken through different filters, for example blue, green and red.

**Photometry**, the careful measurement of how much light comes from an object, is sometimes counted as a fourth category, but modern detectors do it at the same time as imaging, spectroscopy or monitoring, so it is often grouped with imaging.

img.alt: Five coloured filter discs labelled B, U, V, I and R above a graph of the transmission of the Johnson and Bessel U, B, V, R and I filters against wavelength.

steps.title: Filters and passbands
bullets: Each filter lets through a **passband**, a particular range of wavelengths.
A standard set, in order of increasing wavelength, is U (ultraviolet), B (blue), V (visual, yellow-green), R (red) and I (near-infrared).
Comparing an object's brightness in two filters measures its colour, for example B minus V, which for a star is a clue to its temperature.

img.alt: A collage of colourful astronomical images, including nebulae, a supernova remnant and colliding galaxies, with a note that colour often stands for non-visible wavelengths.

steps.title: Pictures of invisible light: colour as a code
bullets: Many astronomical images are made with **invisible light** recorded by special detectors.
Think of a medical X-ray of your arm: you are looking at a record of where X-rays struck the detector, not at the X-rays. Images from the Chandra X-Ray Observatory are made in the same way.

Invisible light has no natural colour, because colour is a property of visible light only. Astronomers **colour-code** such images to stand for the wavelength, the energy or the intensity of the light, or a physical property of the object.
So red in an X-ray image does not mean the object is red. In one Chandra image red marks the lowest-energy X-rays and blue the highest; you always need to know what the colours were chosen to show.

img.alt: A plot of star luminosity against colour (B minus V) for many stars in a cluster, with the main sequence, giants, supergiants and white dwarfs labelled.

steps.title: What images and photometry tell us
bullets: Images and brightness measurements find new objects and give their shape, apparent size, structure, brightness and colour, and, with extra information, luminosity, distance, size and the orbital periods of star systems.

Plotting luminosity against colour (B minus V) for many stars in a cluster sorts them into the main sequence, giants, supergiants and white dwarfs, and reveals properties of the whole cluster, such as its distance.
Only an image shows how big something looks in the sky (its angular size) and its shape; a spectrum alone cannot.

boxes.text: A detector cannot tell colours apart; it only counts photons. Filters make it measure one band at a time, and comparing or combining the bands gives colour.
Imaging = WHERE and what it LOOKS like. Spectroscopy = WHAT it is made of and how it MOVES. Time monitoring = WHEN and how it CHANGES.

Colours in X-ray, infrared or radio images are a code chosen by astronomers; they say nothing by themselves about the object's true colour or temperature. The filter photo on Ch6.2 pt2 slide 3 is labelled B U V I R, but in order of wavelength the passbands run U B V R I.

sections.title: Spectroscopy and spectral resolution

img.alt: A cutaway of a spectrograph attached under a telescope mirror with five labelled stages: slit, collimating mirror, diffraction grating, camera mirror and detector.

steps.title: A spectrograph splits starlight
bullets: A **spectrograph** separates light into its colours (a spectrum) with a **diffraction grating** or a similar device, and records the spectrum with a detector.

The light's path: a narrow **slit** lets in only the light of the object being studied; a collimating mirror makes the rays parallel; the grating spreads them out by wavelength; a camera mirror focuses the spread-out light; the detector records it.
Here the spectrograph hangs under a reflecting telescope and the light enters through the hole in the primary mirror.

steps.title: What a spectrum can tell us
bullets: Plotting the intensity at each wavelength turns the rainbow strip into a graph; dark absorption lines become dips.

A spectrum carries a wealth of information: **chemical composition** (which lines appear), **temperature**, and **motion**: the Doppler shift of the lines gives speed toward or away from us, and lines broadened by spin give a star's rotation rate.

For distant galaxies, the speed of moving away (from the expansion of the universe) also points to their distance. Mass, age and dark matter content are worked out by combining such spectral measurements with other information.
What a spectrum alone cannot give is where things are in the sky: an object's shape or angular size needs an image.

steps.title: Spectral resolution and its price
bullets: Just as an image's detail depends on angular resolution, a spectrum's detail depends on its **spectral resolution**: how close together two spectral lines (two wavelengths) can be and still be seen as separate.
At higher spectral resolution, lines that looked merged into one broad dip show up as separate narrow lines, so we learn more.
The cost: in any given time a telescope gathers a limited amount of light, and higher resolution spreads that light more thinly, so each wavelength receives less.
So a spectrum needs a longer exposure than an image, and a high-resolution spectrum needs a longer exposure than a low-resolution one.

img.alt: A graph of the Sun's spectrum measured at Earth's surface, with labelled absorption lines of calcium, iron, magnesium, sodium and hydrogen and Earth-atmosphere oxygen and water lines.

steps.title: Reading a real spectrum
bullets: The Sun's spectrum measured at Earth's surface shows lines from the Sun's own gases (such as hydrogen, sodium, magnesium, iron and calcium).
It also shows lines from oxygen and water vapour in our own air, which absorbs some of the sunlight on the way down.
Astronomers must tell the star's fingerprints apart from the atmosphere's, one more problem that a telescope in space avoids.

boxes.text: Every element absorbs and emits its own set of wavelengths, and motion shifts the whole set. So the positions and shapes of lines tell you what an object is made of, how hot it is and how it moves, without going there.
Angular resolution splits OBJECTS in the sky; spectral resolution splits LINES in a spectrum. More spread = more detail = more exposure time.

Spectroscopy alone can give composition, surface temperature, speed toward or away, and rotation rate, but not the angular size or shape of a galaxy (that needs imaging). Spectral resolution is about close spectral lines, not close stars. Ch6.2 pt2 slide 10 also lists mass, age, distance and dark matter, which are inferred with extra information.

sections.title: Time monitoring, and working with astronomical data

img.alt: A graph of the brightness of the variable star Mira over about 2000 days, rising and falling again and again with a 331 day period marked.

steps.title: Light curves
bullets: Many objects change with time. Some stars have sudden outbursts; most stars, the Sun included, vary as starspots cover more or less of their surface; some objects vary in a regular cycle.
**Time monitoring** tracks these changes. The results are usually shown as a **light curve**, a graph of brightness against time.
The star Mira rises and falls in brightness by more than a factor of 100, with an average period of 331 days, a little under a year.

Some things can only be measured this way: the rate at which a variable star brightens and dims needs brightness recorded and compared at many different times. One image or one spectrum is a single moment.

steps.title: Slow changes and fast changes
bullets: If an object changes slowly, monitoring it may just mean comparing images or spectra from different nights.
For rapid changes, instruments take many quick exposures, sometimes recording the arrival time of every single photon.
Examples: pulsating Cepheid stars, solar flares that spike in X-rays within minutes, storms on other worlds, asteroids being tracked, and stars slowly moving across the sky over years.

img.alt: Stacked light curves showing small dips in brightness as each of seven TRAPPIST-1 planets crosses its star, next to a picture of the system compared with the inner Solar System.

steps.title: Finding planets by their dips
bullets: Small, regular dips in a star's brightness can reveal an orbiting planet: each time the planet passes in front of the star (a **transit**), it blocks a little of the starlight.
The TRAPPIST-1 system, about 40 light-years away, has seven planets, each making its own repeating dip.
The time between dips gives the planet's orbital period, and the depth of the dip shows how big the planet is compared with its star.

steps.title: Astronomers today work mostly with data
bullets: The **Vera C. Rubin Observatory** in Chile will revolutionise time monitoring. Its very wide view covers the area of nearly 50 full Moons per image, its 3.2-gigapixel camera (nearly 1000 times a phone camera's pixels) takes a 15-second exposure every 20 seconds, and it scans the whole sky visible from Chile every three nights.
Its 10-year survey will produce about 200 petabytes of data, roughly 10 billion typical online photos, far more than people could ever look through.
So most astronomers spend far more time analysing data than at the telescope. The biggest telescopes are run by professional operators, and all space telescopes are run remotely.
Many astronomers have become 'data miners', using computer and artificial intelligence methods to find discoveries in the flood of data.
Astronomy has three main roles: planning observations, analysing the data, and building theoretical models to explain them. Large international teams share the work.

boxes.text: A single snapshot cannot show change. To know how fast or how often something varies you must measure it again and again and line the measurements up in time.
Light curve = brightness against TIME; spectrum = brightness against WAVELENGTH. Don't mix up the two axes.

Only time monitoring can measure how quickly a variable star brightens and dims; a planet's colour, a cloud's shape or the number of stars in a cluster come from single images. The gap between transit dips is the orbital period, not the length of one dip.

sections.title: How Earth's atmosphere affects ground-based telescopes

steps.title: Why most telescopes are still on the ground
bullets: Even in the space age, most observatories are on Earth's surface, mainly because for any given size a ground telescope is far cheaper to build, run and repair than one in space.
Daylight: sunlight scattered by the air makes the daytime sky so bright that it hides the faint light from most astronomical objects, so visible-light observing really works only at night.
Weather: even at night, clouds block the view, so you need a clear sky. Air barely scatters radio waves, so radio telescopes can work day and night and even through clouds.
Beyond limiting when we can observe, the atmosphere causes three lasting problems: light pollution, blurring by moving air, and blocking most kinds of light completely.

img.alt: A night-time map of Earth showing bright clusters of city lights in North America, Europe and Asia and dark areas elsewhere.

steps.title: Light pollution
bullets: The air scatters city lights at night just as it scatters sunlight by day. The resulting glow of the night sky is **light pollution**: human-made light that brightens the sky and hides faint objects.
It is why you see far fewer stars from a big city than from the countryside.

As cities grow, they creep toward observatories. The 2.5 m telescope on Mount Wilson, the largest in the world in 1917, would be much more useful without the lights of Los Angeles; Palomar and Kitt Peak are affected less severely.
Many communities now work to cut wasted outdoor lighting, which helps everyone who enjoys a dark sky.

img.alt: A star field crossed by many thin straight streaks left by satellites during a long exposure.

steps.title: Satellite trails
bullets: A newer kind of light pollution comes from satellites in low orbit, which reflect sunlight, especially around twilight. You can tell a satellite by its steady motion against the stars.
Moving satellites leave streaks across long-exposure images.

Internet satellite 'constellations' such as Starlink and OneWeb have already put thousands of satellites in orbit, and more than 100,000 have been proposed. Astronomers are negotiating with companies and governments to limit the damage, which also changes the night sky that everyone sees.

img.alt: Two images of the same bright star: a blurry blob seen with a ground-based telescope and a sharp point seen with the Hubble Space Telescope.

steps.title: Moving air makes stars twinkle and blurs images
bullets: The air above us is constantly churning (**turbulence**), and this moving air bends starlight in ever-changing ways, much as objects above the surface seem to wobble when you gaze up from underwater in a swimming pool.
That jiggling is the **twinkling** of stars. It is pretty, but it blurs telescope images: most ground telescopes cannot do better than about 0.5 arcsecond, however small their diffraction limit.
Twinkling is not a change in the star. Stars twinkle more on windy nights and near the horizon, where their light crosses more air, and they do not twinkle at all in space.
Planets twinkle too, but less than stars, because they appear as tiny discs rather than points, so the small shifts are minor compared with the size of the planet's image.

img.alt: Four photos of mountaintop observatories: Mauna Kea in Hawaii, Cerro Tololo in Chile, Kitt Peak in Arizona and the Nordic Optical Telescope in the Canary Islands.

steps.title: Choosing a site: calm, dark, high, dry
bullets: Astronomers soften these problems by choosing sites that are **dark** (little light pollution), **dry** (few clouds and little rain), **calm** (little turbulence) and **high** (above part of the atmosphere).

A handful of sites satisfy all four unusually well, so many of the most powerful telescopes on Earth are built there: the 4300 m summit of Maunakea in Hawai'i, a 2400 m site on La Palma in the Canary Islands, and the 2600 m Paranal site in Chile.
Other famous sites in the photos are Kitt Peak in Arizona and Cerro Tololo in Chile.
A mountaintop helps with light pollution, twinkling and some infrared light, but no mountain is high enough to receive ultraviolet light or X-rays.

Calm, Dark, High, Dry: the four words that describe every great observing site.

Stars twinkle because moving air in OUR atmosphere bends their light, not because the stars change, not because of gas between the stars and not because of our eyes. Light pollution means human-made light scattered in the sky, not industry or harmful gases. A remote mountain site does NOT allow ultraviolet or X-ray observations.

sections.title: Adaptive optics, and why we put telescopes in space

img.alt: Two false-colour star images: without adaptive optics a single blurry glow, and with adaptive optics two separate bright stars.

steps.title: Adaptive optics undoes the twinkle
bullets: **Adaptive optics** greatly reduces the blurring caused by turbulence. The moving air makes the starlight dance around; adaptive optics makes one of the telescope's mirrors do the opposite dance, cancelling the distortion.
Tiny motors called actuators slightly reshape a mirror, usually the secondary or a later smaller one, many times every second.

A computer figures out each correction by tracking how the image of a nearby bright star is distorted. When no such star is close to the target, the observatory beams a laser upward to make an artificial 'star' it can track.
In this pair of near-infrared images, a double star whose stars are 0.28 arcsecond apart looks like one blurry star without adaptive optics and like two clear stars with it.

It fixes blurring only. It does not add collecting area, increase magnification, remove clouds or light pollution, or let blocked wavelengths through, and it is used on ground telescopes, not space ones.

img.alt: Pictures of the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope in orbit above Earth.

steps.title: Why go to space?
bullets: The ultimate escape from the atmosphere's problems is to go above it. With no blurring, twinkling, weather or light pollution, the Hubble Space Telescope has been hugely successful even though its mirror is only 2.4 m wide.

The bigger reason, though: most kinds of light never make it down to the ground. Only radio waves, visible light (plus the very longest ultraviolet) and small parts of the infrared get through, and the air itself glows in the infrared.
Hubble observes infrared and ultraviolet as well as visible light. Most objects give off light over a broad range of wavelengths, so to understand them we need telescopes in space.
The costs: space telescopes are expensive, their mirror size is limited by what a rocket can carry, and they are very hard to repair. Hubble's last servicing mission was in 2009.

steps.title: The James Webb Space Telescope: built for infrared
bullets: At 6.5 m across, JWST's mirror is 2.7 times wider than Hubble's, so it gathers over 7 times as much light (2.7² ≈ 7.3) and can make out finer detail.
The mirror is made of 18 hexagonal segments, folded to fit inside the rocket, then unfolded in space and carefully adjusted until its vision was as sharp as physics allows.

It orbits about 1.5 million km from Earth, at a point called L2, where one huge **sunshield** can always block the light of both the Sun and Earth. That keeps the telescope cold, so its own heat (infrared glow) does not swamp what it is trying to see.

Goal 1: the most distant galaxies. For galaxies farther than about 12 billion light-years, the expansion of the universe has moved nearly all of their starlight into the infrared, where Hubble has trouble seeing. JWST can pick up galaxies from a time when the universe was just a few hundred million years old.
Goal 2: exoplanets. Planets are cool and give off mainly infrared light (their visible light is only reflected starlight), so studying a planet's own glow means observing in the infrared.

steps.title: What space does NOT do
bullets: A common mistake is to think space telescopes see better because they are 'closer to the stars'. On a scale where Earth is 1 mm across, JWST is only about 15 cm away, while the nearest stars are thousands of kilometres away. The distance to the stars is effectively the same.
All the advantages of a space telescope come from being above the atmosphere: no turbulent blurring and access to every wavelength.

Being in space does not make a small mirror collect more light. For visible light, a large ground telescope still collects more light; the space telescope wins on sharpness and on blocked wavelengths.

Wavelengths that the air blocks need space: the hot outer layers of stars like the Sun give off ultraviolet and X-rays, so do neutron stars and black holes, and violent cosmic events release bursts of gamma rays.

boxes.text: Adaptive optics fights the blur from the air; a space telescope escapes it completely and also escapes the air's absorption of most wavelengths.
Adaptive optics = anti-wobble mirror: it fixes blur and nothing else. Space = no air: no blur AND all wavelengths.

The best reason to put a visible-light telescope in space is that it sits above the turbulent air, so the light is not distorted. It is NOT closer to the stars, NOT about earthquakes, and big telescopes are NOT easier to build in space. Adaptive optics reduces turbulence blur for ground telescopes; linking telescopes is interferometry, and more collecting area needs a bigger mirror.

sections.title: Observing invisible light: what reaches the ground, radio and infrared

img.alt: A graph of how opaque Earth's atmosphere is at each wavelength from gamma rays to long radio waves, showing windows for visible light and radio waves and blocked regions elsewhere.

steps.title: The atmosphere is a filter
bullets: Different kinds of light reach different depths in the air. The ground receives only **radio waves**, **visible light** (along with the very longest ultraviolet) and a few narrow bands of **infrared**.
Gamma rays, X-rays, most ultraviolet and most infrared are soaked up high in the atmosphere, so observing them requires very high altitudes or space.
The atmosphere is most transparent to visible light: all visible wavelengths get through.
The higher you go, the more infrared you can catch: mountaintops reach a few infrared bands, high-flying aircraft much more.

Infrared and ultraviolet close to the visible behave like visible light and can be focused by ordinary telescope mirrors; that is why Hubble can observe some of both. Other wavelengths need different designs.

img.alt: The Arecibo radio telescope, a huge dish set in a forested hollow in Puerto Rico, with a platform held above it by cables.

steps.title: Radio telescopes
bullets: The satellite TV dish is the world's most common telescope: a little radio telescope. The dish acts as the primary mirror, and the receiver sits in front of it at the focus, where a secondary mirror would otherwise go.

A TV dish points at one fixed satellite and only needs to collect the signal. A research radio telescope follows sources that rise and set, needs a large area to catch faint radio waves, and needs decent resolution because it makes images.

Radio wavelengths are long, so dishes must be enormous to see fine detail: China's 500 m FAST (completed 2016) and Puerto Rico's 305 m Arecibo (collapsed 2020). Even so they resolve only about 1 arcminute, roughly 1000 times worse than Hubble in visible light. That is why the largest telescopes of all are radio telescopes.
Because the waves are so long, the dish need not be perfectly smooth: metal panels or even wire mesh reflect them well.

There is no real advantage to radio telescopes in space (the air does not distort radio waves), but human radio signals are an even worse problem than light pollution. Astronomers hope one day to put radio telescopes on the far side of the Moon, which would block Earth's noise.

img.alt: The SOFIA infrared telescope carried in a Boeing 747 aircraft and the Spitzer Space Telescope in space.

steps.title: Infrared telescopes
bullets: Most infrared light behaves much like visible light, so infrared telescopes look much like visible-light telescopes.

A few infrared bands can be observed from high mountains such as Maunakea. SOFIA (2010-2022) carried a 2.5 m infrared telescope inside a Boeing 747, looking out through a large hole in the plane's side.
The big problem, especially at longer infrared wavelengths: Earth, the air and even the telescope itself give off infrared **thermal radiation** (heat glow) that swamps faint infrared from space.

The only cure is to get away from Earth's heat and keep the telescope very cold. The Spitzer Space Telescope (2003-2020) was cooled with liquid helium to a few degrees above absolute zero; JWST stays cold with its sunshield and distant orbit.

boxes.text: A mirror only has to be smooth compared with the wavelength it reflects. Radio waves are centimetres to metres long, so wire mesh looks like a perfect mirror to them. But long waves also diffract a lot, so radio dishes have to be huge.
The longer the wave, the bigger the dish. The warmer the telescope, the worse its infrared view.

The largest-diameter telescopes are radio telescopes, not visible-light ones. The atmosphere is most transparent to visible light (not ultraviolet, X-rays or most infrared). Ch6.4 slide 2 lists visible, radio and some infrared as getting through; the very longest ultraviolet, right next to the visible, also gets through.

sections.title: Ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes

img.alt: Artist pictures of the planned Canadian ultraviolet telescope CASTOR and the Chandra X-ray Observatory orbiting above Earth.

steps.title: Ultraviolet and X-ray telescopes belong in space
bullets: Much ultraviolet light behaves like visible light and could be focused by ordinary mirrors, but the atmosphere absorbs almost all of it. Ultraviolet telescopes must therefore be in space; a modest telescope in orbit beats any telescope on a mountain.
Right now Hubble is the only major space telescope that observes ultraviolet light, and it will keep working only as long as its machinery lasts. Canada's CASTOR is a planned ultraviolet telescope.
Cosmic X-rays never reach the ground, so X-ray telescopes have to be in space as well; one example is NASA's Chandra X-Ray Observatory.

X-rays come from extremely hot gas, millions of degrees, because hotter things give off shorter wavelengths: the hot outer layers of stars, gas around neutron stars and black holes, and the 10-million-degree gas between the galaxies of a cluster. For gas that hot, an X-ray telescope is the right tool.

img.alt: A cutaway of nested cylindrical X-ray mirrors in which a first set deflects X-rays slightly onto a second set that sends them to a focus 10 metres away.

steps.title: Grazing-incidence mirrors
bullets: X-rays carry enough energy to go into many materials, including living tissue (useful to doctors) and ordinary mirrors (a headache for astronomers).
Focusing X-rays resembles aiming a stream of bullets: shoot them straight at a metal sheet and they punch into it, but tilt the sheet so they barely skim it and they get nudged slightly off course.

**Grazing incidence mirrors** use the same trick: the X-rays strike at a very shallow angle and are nudged toward the focus. Chandra uses nested, tube-shaped mirrors; a first set deflects the X-rays onto a second set, which brings them to a focus about 10 m behind.

Different X-ray telescopes have different strengths: Chandra makes the sharpest images, XMM-Newton's larger collecting area gives more detailed X-ray spectra, eROSITA's wide view has produced the best X-ray map of the whole sky, and NuSTAR studies the highest-energy X-rays around black holes.

img.alt: An artist picture of the Fermi Gamma-ray Observatory, a boxy detector with two solar panels, in space.

steps.title: Gamma rays
bullets: Gamma rays pass even through grazing-incidence mirrors, so they cannot be focused in the usual way.

Gamma-ray observatories use massive detectors instead, which capture the photons and work out the direction each one came from. The Large Area Telescope on the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope (launched 2008) weighs 3 tons.
Gamma rays come from the most violent events in the universe, such as gamma-ray bursts.

boxes.text: A high-energy photon that hits a surface head-on goes straight in, but one that just skims the surface can bounce off. The more energetic the light, the shallower the angle needs to be, until for gamma rays no mirror works at all.
Ultraviolet: mirror OK, but space only. X-ray: space plus grazing mirrors. Gamma: space plus no mirrors at all, just big detectors.

X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors because X-rays would go into a normal mirror. They do not use thick mirrors, they are not 'impossible to focus' (that is gamma rays), and they can do spectroscopy. For ultraviolet, being in space matters more than size: a 2.5 m space telescope beats a 30 m mountain telescope.

sections.title: Making telescopes work together: interferometry

img.alt: Several large radio dishes of the Very Large Array standing on the New Mexico plain at sunset.

steps.title: Linking dishes: the Very Large Array
bullets: Every telescope has limits: the diffraction limit fixes the best resolution for its size, and money and technology limit how big it can be built.
Grouping telescopes can't change one fact: together they collect only as much light as their separate areas added up.

But resolution can be improved. In the 1950s radio astronomers learned to link telescopes so that together they reach the angular resolution of one much larger telescope, roughly as wide as the distance between them. This is **interferometry**: it times exactly when the waves arrive at each dish and uses computers to combine the resulting interference patterns.

The Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array in New Mexico has 27 dishes that move along Y-shaped railway tracks. Their combined area equals a single dish 130 m across, but spread out as far as possible they match the resolution of a single dish almost 40 km across.
Linking radio telescopes around the world gives even sharper resolution.

img.alt: The four large domed telescopes of the Very Large Telescope on a mountaintop in Chile's Atacama desert.

steps.title: Interferometry at shorter wavelengths
bullets: Interferometry is harder for shorter wavelengths, but it works. ALMA, on a 5000 m high plateau in Chile, combines 66 telescopes observing millimetre and submillimetre waves.

The **Event Horizon Telescope** linked ALMA with other radio telescopes around the globe to image the shadow of the supermassive black hole at the centre of galaxy M87, and later the one at the centre of our Milky Way.

Infrared and visible interferometry is now done too: telescopes are built in pairs (Keck, Magellan) or on one shared mount (the Large Binocular Telescope), and the four 8.2 m units of the Very Large Telescope in Chile can be combined.
Astronomers are testing ways to extend interferometry to X-rays, and hope one day to build giant interferometers in space or on the Moon.

boxes.text: Resolution depends on how wide a telescope is, because diffraction depends on the size of the opening. Two dishes far apart sample the incoming waves across that whole width, so they act like one huge opening for detail, but they still catch only the light that falls on their own surfaces.
Interferometry = sharper, NOT brighter. Resolution ~ spacing; light = sum of the dishes.

Interferometry lets linked telescopes see detail as finely as one far bigger telescope would, but it does not give them that telescope's light-collecting area. Two 10 m dishes 100 m apart resolve like a 100 m dish but collect only twice the light of one 10 m dish. It is not about chemical composition, light pollution, or using one telescope for radio and visible light.

sections.title: Other cosmic messengers: neutrinos, cosmic rays and gravitational waves

steps.title: Neutrinos
bullets: A **neutrino** is an extremely lightweight subatomic particle, not a form of light.
Neutrinos are made in nuclear reactions, including the fusion in the Sun's core and the reactions in exploding stars.

They pass through almost all matter, even whole planets, so very few are ever caught. 'Neutrino telescopes' are therefore huge detectors placed deep in mines or under water or ice; IceCube's detectors hang 1.5 to 2.5 km deep in the ice at the South Pole.
They have already taught us a lot about the Sun and about exploding stars.

steps.title: Cosmic rays
bullets: **Cosmic rays** are very-high-energy subatomic particles from space that continually strike Earth.
Despite the name they are not rays of light: they are particles, not electromagnetic waves.
No one fully understands where they come from yet, but some, at least, are produced by supernovas: massive stars blowing up at the end of their lives.
Astronomers catch and study them with detectors on satellites and on the ground.

steps.title: Gravitational waves
bullets: Einstein's general theory of relativity predicts **gravitational waves**: ripples in space itself. They are not a form of light, yet they move at light's speed.
They are not a form of light of any energy, high or low.
Observatories such as LIGO (two detectors, in Hanford, Washington and Livingston, Louisiana, working with Virgo in Italy) now detect them regularly.
The sources detected so far are all pairs of neutron stars and black holes that were orbiting each other and merged.

steps.title: Why several messengers?
bullets: Light remains our main source of information, but these other messengers carry information that light alone cannot.
Neutrinos escape straight from the Sun's core, and gravitational waves come from black-hole mergers that may give off no light at all.
Seeing the same event with light and another messenger gives two independent views of it.
The big picture: technology drives discovery. Each bigger telescope, more sensitive detector, new wavelength or new messenger has taught us more about the universe.

boxes.text: Light can be absorbed, blocked or simply never produced. Particles and gravitational waves are made and travel differently, so they reach us from places and events that light cannot show.
Two particles and one wave, and none of them is light: neutrinos (light, sneaky particles), cosmic rays (fast, charged particles), gravitational waves (ripples in space).

Neutrinos are lightweight subatomic particles, not very-high- or very-low-energy light. Cosmic rays are high-energy particles, not electromagnetic waves. Gravitational waves are not light at all; they come from sources such as merging neutron stars and black holes. These topics are not on the Ch6.4 slides but are in the assigned reading.

cards.back: The width (diameter) of a telescope's primary lens or mirror. It sets how much light the telescope can collect, because the light-collecting area is proportional to the diameter squared.
cards.short: Width of the main mirror or lens

cards.back: The smallest angle between two objects at which a telescope can still show them as separate, usually measured in arcseconds. A smaller angle means finer detail. Diffraction limits it: it is proportional to wavelength divided by diameter.
cards.short: Smaller minimum angle means finer detail

cards.back: Measuring how much light is received from an astronomical object, often through coloured filters. It gives brightness and colour and, with other information, luminosity, distance and size.
cards.short: Measures brightness, often through filters

cards.back: Spreading light into a spectrum and measuring its intensity at each wavelength. The pattern reveals chemical composition, temperature and motion.
cards.short: Wavelength patterns reveal composition, temperature, motion

cards.back: A graph of an object's brightness measured over time. It shows repeating changes such as variable stars, planet transits and flares.
cards.short: Brightness versus time

cards.back: Changing the shape of a telescope mirror many times a second to cancel part of the blurring caused by turbulent air. It sharpens images but does not collect more light or remove clouds.
cards.short: Mirror reshaped to cancel some turbulence blur

cards.back: Linking two or more telescopes so that together they give the angular resolution of a single telescope as wide as their spacing. It sharpens detail; the light collected is only the sum of the individual telescopes.
cards.short: Linked telescopes resolve finer detail

cards.back: Charge-coupled device: a grid of pixels that turn arriving photons into electrons. The charge in each pixel is read out and counted to make an image. Used in phones and telescopes.
cards.short: A pixel sensor that counts photons

cards.back: A detector, often deep underground or in water or ice, that waits for the rare interactions of neutrinos arriving from space. IceCube in Antarctic ice is an example.
cards.short: Huge detector for rare neutrino hits

cards.back: A ripple in spacetime made by accelerating masses, such as merging neutron stars or black holes. It travels at the speed of light but is not light.
cards.short: A spacetime ripple, not light

cards.back: A very high-energy subatomic particle arriving from space. It is not light. Magnetic fields bend the paths of charged cosmic rays, so their arrival direction does not point back to the source.
cards.short: A fast space particle, not light

cards.back: The flat surface through the focal point, at right angles to the optical axis. For distant objects, the focused image forms here and a detector placed here records it.
cards.short: Where distant objects come into focus

cards.back: The best angular resolution a telescope can reach if it is limited only by the wave nature (interference) of light. It gets smaller (better) with larger diameter and shorter wavelength.
cards.short: Wave limit on resolving detail

cards.back: A lens defect: refraction depends on wavelength, so different colours focus at slightly different places and bright objects get coloured fringes. Mirrors do not have it.
cards.short: A lens focuses colours at different places

cards.back: An instrument that uses a slit, a diffraction grating and a detector to spread light into a spectrum and record it.
cards.short: Separates and records wavelengths

cards.back: A range of wavelengths that passes through Earth's atmosphere well enough to be observed from the ground: visible light, radio waves and a few narrow infrared bands.
cards.short: A wavelength range that reaches the ground

cards.back: Nested mirrors hit at a very shallow angle, which deflect X-rays gradually to a focus. X-rays would pass into or through an ordinary mirror.
cards.short: Shallow-angle mirrors focus X-rays

cards.back: An extremely light subatomic particle made in nuclear reactions, including fusion in the Sun and exploding stars. It passes through matter with almost no interaction.
cards.short: A ghost-like particle from nuclear reactions

cards.back: A detector, such as LIGO, that sends laser light along long perpendicular arms and measures the tiny change in their lengths as a gravitational wave passes.
cards.short: Laser arms measure tiny length changes

cards.back: The place behind a lens or mirror where light from an object comes into focus. A screen, retina or detector must sit here to record a sharp image. A single convex lens makes an upside-down image there.
cards.short: Where the focused image forms

cards.back: The point where parallel rays from a very distant object meet after passing through a convex lens or reflecting from a concave mirror.
cards.short: Where parallel rays meet

cards.back: A box with a tiny hole instead of a lens. Each point of the scene sends one thin ray through the hole, so the image is sharp but dim, flipped left-right and upside down.
cards.short: Tiny hole: sharp but dim image

cards.back: The distance from a lens or mirror to its focal point.
cards.short: Distance from lens to focal point

cards.back: A lens thicker in the middle than at the edges. It refracts parallel rays to a focus and forms an upside-down image. Eyes and refracting telescopes use one.
cards.short: Bends rays together by refraction

cards.back: A mirror curved inward. It brings parallel rays to a focus by reflection, on the same side as the incoming light. It is the primary mirror of a reflecting telescope.
cards.short: Focuses by reflection

cards.back: How much of the scene, in distance, is in sharp focus. A larger lens diameter gives more light but a shallower depth of field.
cards.short: Range of distances in sharp focus

cards.back: The length of time the shutter is open, letting light build up on the detector. Longer exposures gather more total light and reveal fainter detail, but very bright areas can overexpose.
cards.short: Time the detector collects light

cards.back: One picture element of a detector. It accumulates charge from arriving photons, and the charge is measured to count how much light landed there.
cards.short: One light-counting square of a detector

cards.back: The area of a telescope's primary mirror or lens that gathers light: A = πD²/4, so it is proportional to the diameter squared. Doubling the diameter gives 4 times the light.
cards.short: Proportional to diameter squared

cards.back: The angle between two objects as seen by an observer. It shrinks as the pair moves farther away. A telescope shows them as two only if the separation is larger than its angular resolution.
cards.short: Angle between two objects

cards.back: The pattern a telescope makes from a single point of light, a bright centre with rings or blotches caused by diffraction. It can be minimised but never removed.
cards.short: Diffraction pattern of a star

cards.back: A telescope that focuses light with a large lens. Big lenses are heavy, held only at the edge, and show chromatic aberration, so research telescopes are rarely refractors.
cards.short: Uses a lens to focus

cards.back: A telescope that focuses light with a curved primary mirror and a smaller secondary mirror. The mirror can be supported from behind or built from segments, so virtually all large telescopes are reflectors.
cards.short: Uses mirrors to focus

cards.back: A reflecting-telescope design in which the secondary mirror sends the light back down through a hole in the primary mirror to instruments underneath. In a Newtonian design the light goes out the side instead.
cards.short: Light exits through a hole in the primary

cards.back: A large mirror built from many smaller pieces that work as one. Each Keck telescope has 36 hexagons, JWST has 18 and the Extremely Large Telescope will have 798.
cards.short: Many small mirrors acting as one

cards.back: The range of wavelengths a filter lets through, such as the U, B, V, R and I filters.
cards.short: Wavelength range of one filter

cards.back: Colour assigned to stand for something other than the true colour: the wavelength, energy or intensity of invisible light. Colour is a property of visible light only.
cards.short: Colour used as a code

cards.back: How close together two spectral lines can be and still be seen as separate. Higher resolution shows more detail but spreads the light out and needs a longer exposure.
cards.short: Ability to separate close spectral lines

cards.back: A planet passing in front of its star, which blocks a small part of the starlight. The light curve shows a dip that repeats every orbit.
cards.short: A repeating dip in a star's light

cards.back: Human-made light that scatters in the atmosphere and brightens the night sky, making faint objects harder to see. Satellite trails add to the problem.
cards.short: Artificial light that brightens the sky

cards.back: The flickering of a star seen through the atmosphere. Moving air refracts the light in random directions. It does not happen in space.
cards.short: Turbulent air bending starlight

cards.back: A large metal dish or mesh that reflects radio waves to a receiver at its focus. The long wavelengths mean it need not be perfectly smooth, but it must be huge for good resolution.
cards.short: Big dish or mesh for radio waves

cards.back: A space telescope with a 6.5 m mirror of 18 hexagonal segments, observing mainly infrared light from far beyond the Moon behind a large sunshield that keeps it cold.
cards.short: Cold 6.5 m infrared space telescope
