cards.back: A 40 m radio dish collects 16 times the light of a 10 m telescope (area goes as D squared), but at 1 m wavelength its resolution is far worse, because the smallest angle goes as wavelength over D.
cards.short: 16x area, much blurrier

cards.back: Linking several telescopes so they act like one much wider dish, sharpening angular resolution. It does not remove the blurring caused by the atmosphere.
cards.short: Linked telescopes: sharper, not less blur

quiz.q: An astronomer needs to record a very dim nebula without changing the exposure time. Which telescope change most directly improves the number of source photons reaching the detector?
options: Use a larger primary aperture
Increase magnification alone
Move the detector farther from the focal plane
Observe from a lower, wetter site
quiz.why: A larger aperture has more area to catch photons, and that is what a dim nebula needs. Magnification only enlarges the picture, moving the detector off the focal plane blurs it, and a lower, wetter site puts more absorbing, turbulent air in the way.

quiz.q: Two stars blur into one spot in a telescope image, although the combined image is bright. Which property is most directly limiting the ability to distinguish the stars?
options: Angular resolution
Total image brightness
The detector's colour balance
The observing schedule
quiz.why: Angular resolution is the smallest angle at which two sources show as separate. A bright combined image shows there is enough light, so brightness is not the problem, and neither colour balance nor schedule decides whether two points can be told apart.

quiz.q: A telescope records more photons from a faint source, but two close sources remain unresolved. Which interpretation best separates the two outcomes?
options: Light collection improved; resolving power may still be limited.
Both brightness and resolution must have improved equally.
More photons guarantee unlimited resolution.
The detector has become a spectrograph.
quiz.why: Light collection and resolution are separate properties. More photons make a source brighter, but two sources still blur together if their separation is smaller than the angular resolution. More light does not remove the diffraction or turbulence limit.
quiz.source: Ch6.2 pt1 slides 2 and 4; Cosmic Perspective 6.2

quiz.q: A planet passes in front of its star, producing a repeated dip in measured brightness. Which data product is best suited to reveal the event?
options: A light curve from time monitoring
One spectrum without time information
A single image without calibrated brightness
A mirror's focal-plane diagram
quiz.why: A light curve tracks brightness over time, so recurring transits show up as repeated dips. One spectrum or one image is a single moment and cannot show a repeating change, and a focal-plane diagram describes the optics, not the star.

quiz.q: A star's spectrum contains a recognizable pattern of absorption lines shifted from the laboratory pattern. Which combined inference is most justified?
options: Its chemical composition and motion can be investigated.
Its physical diameter is measured directly from the line pattern.
The star's image must have been recorded only in radio waves.
The shift proves that Earth's atmosphere created the star.
quiz.why: Which lines appear tells you the elements present, and the shift of the lines (the Doppler effect) tells you about motion toward or away from us. A spectrum does not give a star's diameter directly, and the shift says nothing about radio waves or the atmosphere.

quiz.q: An observatory has clear skies but severe city glow and turbulent air. Which site change would address both problems most directly?
options: Move to a dark, calm location, preferably at high elevation.
Use a longer focal length at the same site.
Replace the mirror with a larger screen.
Observe through more atmosphere to average out distortions.
quiz.why: A dark site cuts light pollution, and a calm, high site means less turbulent air above the telescope. A longer focal length does not change either problem, and looking through more air makes both turbulence and sky glow worse.

quiz.q: Adaptive optics sharpens a stellar image at a windy observatory. Which limitation remains even after the mirror is adjusted?
options: Clouds and light pollution are not removed by correcting turbulence.
The technique changes a planet's orbital path.
The atmosphere becomes transparent to every wavelength.
The telescope no longer needs a detector.
quiz.why: Adaptive optics cancels part of the blurring from turbulent air. It cannot remove clouds, sky glow or atmospheric absorption, and the telescope still needs a detector to record the image.

quiz.q: A ground observatory is designed to study ultraviolet radiation, but no signal from the target reaches it. Which explanation and response best fit?
options: The atmosphere absorbs much ultraviolet; place the instrument above most of the atmosphere.
Ultraviolet exists only at night; increase the exposure.
Mirrors cannot reflect ultraviolet; use a larger dish on the ground.
The target emits only visible light; measure a light curve.
quiz.why: Earth's atmosphere absorbs most ultraviolet light, so it never reaches the ground and a space telescope is needed. A longer exposure cannot collect light that has been absorbed, ultraviolet near the visible range can be focused by mirrors, and a light curve does not change what wavelengths arrive.

quiz.q: Several radio dishes are linked so their observations behave like a much wider instrument. Which capability is principally improved?
options: Angular resolution
The total collecting area beyond the sum of the dishes
Atmospheric transmission at X-ray wavelengths
The temperature of the radio source
quiz.why: Interferometry gives the angular resolution of a telescope as wide as the spread of the dishes. The collecting area is only the sum of the dishes, the atmosphere is unchanged, and the source's temperature is not affected by how we observe it.

quiz.q: Why does a neutrino detector monitor a very large volume of ice or water rather than relying on an ordinary optical telescope?
options: Neutrinos interact rarely, so a huge target volume increases the chance of detecting an interaction.
Neutrinos are visible only when reflected from a mirror.
Water forces all neutrinos to stop before reaching the detector.
Optical telescopes cannot record any particles.
quiz.why: A neutrino usually passes through matter without a trace. Only a huge amount of material gives a reasonable chance of catching an occasional interaction. Neutrinos are not light and do not reflect from mirrors, and water does not stop them.

quiz.q: A laser interferometer registers a signal that changes the relative lengths of its perpendicular arms by a tiny amount. What is the intended interpretation?
options: A gravitational wave has changed spacetime distances.
Atmospheric absorption has changed a star's spectrum.
A cosmic ray has become a visible-light image.
The observatory has measured a planet's surface temperature.
quiz.why: A passing gravitational wave stretches and squeezes distances by a tiny amount, which laser interferometers such as LIGO can measure. The other options describe spectra, cosmic rays or temperature, none of which change the arm lengths.

quiz.q: A lens-based instrument produces slightly different focus positions for blue and red light. Which design change most directly avoids this particular image defect?
options: Use a reflecting telescope.
Increase the camera's colour saturation.
Add a radio receiver.
Place the detector outside the focal plane.
quiz.why: This defect is chromatic aberration: refraction depends on wavelength, so a lens focuses colours at different places. A mirror reflects every colour at the same angle. Image colour settings, radio receivers and misplacing the detector do not fix it.

quiz.q: Light rays from a distant point are reflected correctly by the primary mirror, but the recorded image is still blurred because the sensor is misplaced. What should be corrected?
options: Put the detector at the focal plane.
Increase the target's apparent angular size.
Use a second light curve.
Move the telescope below the atmosphere.
quiz.why: The detector must sit where the optics bring the light into focus. The target's size, a light curve and the atmosphere do not matter when the sensor is simply in the wrong place.

quiz.q: A researcher wants both a sky image and a quantitative brightness comparison between two stars. Which statement about the measurements is most accurate?
options: Imaging records spatial information; photometry quantifies received light.
Photometry reveals only the stars' chemical elements.
An image cannot contain brightness information.
A spectrum and a light curve are interchangeable.
quiz.why: An image shows where light arrives, and photometry measures how much of it. Chemical elements come from spectra, images do contain brightness, and a spectrum (intensity against wavelength) is not a light curve (intensity against time).

quiz.q: A colourful image combines observations at wavelengths invisible to the human eye. Which interpretation is scientifically sound?
options: Colours may be assigned to show data from non-visible wavelengths.
Every displayed colour must be directly visible to the eye in the original radiation.
The image cannot represent real astronomical measurements.
The detector must have changed the source's physical colour.
quiz.why: Invisible light has no natural colour, so astronomers assign colours to stand for wavelength, energy or intensity. The image is still real data. The detector does not change the source, and the colours are a code, not what an eye would see.

quiz.q: A ground telescope detects visible light and radio waves but not most X-rays from a target. Which factor best explains this pattern?
options: Earth's atmosphere has different transmission windows at different wavelengths.
The target emits X-rays only when observed from the ground.
Visible and radio light do not interact with detectors.
X-rays have no measurable energy.
quiz.why: The atmosphere lets some wavelength ranges through (visible, radio) and absorbs others, including X-rays. The target does not depend on where we observe it, and X-rays carry a lot of energy.

quiz.q: An X-ray instrument uses nested mirrors at shallow angles. Why is this geometry useful?
options: X-rays can reflect at grazing incidence even though they penetrate ordinary mirrors.
X-rays behave exactly like visible light in a flat mirror.
Shallow angles turn X-rays into radio waves.
The mirrors block all high-energy photons.
quiz.why: X-rays go into or through an ordinary mirror, like bullets hitting a metal sheet head-on. At a very shallow angle they graze the surface and are gradually deflected toward a focus. They are not changed into radio waves and the mirrors do not block them.

quiz.q: A radio array has excellent detail but only modest total photon collection. Which statement best explains how this is possible?
options: A long interferometer baseline can improve resolution without increasing total collecting area beyond the dishes.
High resolution always proves that the array has a huge collecting area.
Radio waves are unaffected by aperture size.
Interferometry changes the wavelength of the source.
quiz.why: The spacing of the dishes sets the resolving detail, while the light collected is just the sum of the individual dishes. Good resolution does not prove a huge collecting area, and observing method never changes the source's wavelength.

quiz.q: A neutrino from a stellar explosion crosses a planet without being absorbed. Which property explains why a detector must search for rare events?
options: Neutrinos interact very weakly with matter.
Neutrinos are identical to photons.
Neutrinos are blocked by visible-light filters.
Neutrinos orbit the detector.
quiz.why: Neutrinos hardly interact with matter, so they travel through planets, but that also makes them very hard to catch. They are not photons, and they are not stopped by filters or bound to the detector.

quiz.q: A high-energy charged particle arrives from a distant source after passing through galactic magnetic fields. Why may its arrival direction not point back to the source?
options: Magnetic fields can bend the particle's path.
Its path is focused by a refracting telescope.
The atmosphere turns it into a neutrino.
It always follows Earth's orbital plane.
quiz.why: Cosmic rays are charged particles, and magnetic fields bend their paths as they travel. Light is not bent this way. Telescopes and the atmosphere do not control the direction they came from.

quiz.q: An event is observed in visible light and later by a gravitational-wave detector. Why is the combined observation valuable?
options: Different messengers provide complementary evidence about the same event.
The gravitational-wave signal is just a coloured optical image.
Only the visible-light observation can carry information.
The observations must have come from unrelated sources.
quiz.why: Light and gravitational waves carry different kinds of information, so together they constrain the event better than either alone. A gravitational wave is not light, and both signals carry information.

quiz.q: A telescope is moved to orbit to study a wavelength strongly absorbed by the atmosphere. Which benefit is most directly expected?
options: More of that incoming radiation can reach the detector.
The target's intrinsic luminosity increases.
The orbiting telescope no longer needs calibration.
Every wavelength becomes equally easy to observe.
quiz.why: Above the atmosphere, wavelengths that the air absorbs can reach the telescope. The source itself is unchanged, calibration is still needed, and some wavelengths are still harder to observe than others.

quiz.q: A camera takes exposures through separate filters and combines them into a colour image. What must be considered when interpreting its colours?
options: The displayed colours may encode filter measurements rather than a single direct-eye view.
Each pixel must have measured every wavelength simultaneously.
The filters remove all information about brightness.
The colours prove the source is inside Earth's atmosphere.
quiz.why: Each exposure measures only one passband, and the combined colours come from mapping those measurements to displayed colours. A filter does not remove brightness information, and the colours say nothing about where the source is.

quiz.q: Which observing plan would best distinguish a changing star's brightness from its chemical composition?
options: Use repeated brightness measurements for a light curve and a spectrograph for wavelength patterns.
Use one uncalibrated image for both measurements.
Use only an interferometer baseline measurement.
Use a mirror test and assume the spectrum.
quiz.why: Brightness change needs repeated measurements over time (a light curve), and composition needs the wavelength pattern (a spectrum). A single image cannot give either, and interferometry is about resolution.

quiz.q: Two otherwise identical telescopes observe the same wavelength. Telescope B has twice the aperture diameter of telescope A. Which combination best describes the main effects?
options: B collects about twice as much light and has twice the resolving power.
B collects about four times as much light and can resolve details about half as large.
B collects the same amount of light but has four times the resolving power.
B collects about half as much light and resolves details twice as large.
Neither light gathering nor resolution depends on aperture.
quiz.why: Light-gathering area scales with diameter squared, so doubling the diameter collects four times as much light. At a fixed wavelength the smallest resolvable angle is proportional to 1/D, so details about half as large can be distinguished. The other options mix up the square law with the simple one.
quiz.source: Ch6.2 pt1 slides 2 and 5; Cosmic Perspective 6.2

quiz.q: A faint galaxy needs a 16-hour exposure on a 3 m telescope to collect enough light for a good image. Using the same detector under the same conditions, about how long would a 12 m telescope need?
options: 4 hours
1 hour
8 hours
16 hours
64 hours
quiz.why: The diameter is 4 times larger, so the light-collecting area is 4² = 16 times larger and the same total light arrives in 1/16 of the time: 16 hours ÷ 16 = 1 hour. Four hours forgets the square, 16 hours assumes no gain, and 64 hours multiplies instead of dividing.

quiz.q: A telescope's diffraction-limited angular resolution is 0.10 arcsecond for light of wavelength 500 nm. Using the same telescope at 1000 nm, the best possible angular resolution is about
options: 0.05 arcsecond, twice as sharp
0.20 arcsecond, twice as coarse
0.40 arcsecond, four times as coarse
0.10 arcsecond, unchanged
0.025 arcsecond, four times as sharp
quiz.why: The smallest angle is proportional to wavelength divided by diameter. The diameter is the same and the wavelength doubles, so the angle doubles to 0.20 arcsecond and details must be twice as large to be seen. A shorter wavelength would be sharper, 0.40 would square the change, and 0.10 ignores wavelength.

quiz.q: A 2 m telescope has a certain diffraction-limited sharpness at 500 nm. A team plans an infrared telescope for 1500 nm light and wants the same diffraction-limited sharpness. What mirror diameter do they need?
options: 6 m
4 m
2 m
quiz.why: The smallest angle is proportional to λ/D. To keep the angle the same while the wavelength triples, the diameter must triple too: 3 × 2 m = 6 m. The square (18 m), simple addition (4 m), no change (2 m) and dividing (0.67 m) all misuse the proportion.

quiz.q: Two stars are 0.3 arcsecond apart in the sky. Which observation can show them as two separate points of light?
options: A ground-based 10 m telescope in typical turbulent air, which blurs stars to about 0.7 arcsecond
A telescope with a resolution of 1 arcsecond used for a very long exposure
A telescope with a resolution of 0.5 arcsecond, magnifying the image 100 times
A space telescope with an angular resolution of 0.1 arcsecond
A telescope with an angular resolution of 0.4 arcsecond
quiz.why: The telescope's smallest resolvable angle must be smaller than the 0.3 arcsecond separation, and only 0.1 arcsecond qualifies. Turbulence (0.7) and 0.4 and 1 arcsecond are all coarser than the separation. A long exposure gathers more light but does not sharpen, and magnification only enlarges the blur.
quiz.source: Ch6.2 pt1 slide 4; Ch6.3 slide 5; Cosmic Perspective 6.2-6.3

quiz.q: A ground-based 8 m telescope images a double star whose stars are 0.3 arcsecond apart. Turbulence limits the image to about 0.7 arcsecond; with adaptive optics the telescope reaches close to its diffraction limit of about 0.05 arcsecond. What do the two images show?
options: Two separate stars both times, but dimmer without adaptive optics
One blurred blob both times, but brighter with adaptive optics
Without adaptive optics one blurred blob; with it two separate stars
Two separate stars without adaptive optics and one blob with it
Nothing without adaptive optics and one blob with it
quiz.why: Without correction, turbulence spreads each star over about 0.7 arcsecond, bigger than the 0.3 arcsecond gap, so they merge into one blob. Adaptive optics cancels much of the blur, so the resolution is well below 0.3 arcsecond and two stars appear. It does not add photons, so the 'brighter' and 'dimmer' options are wrong.

quiz.q: A star's brightness is measured every few minutes for ten days. The light curve is flat at 100 percent, except that every 4 days the brightness drops sharply to 99 percent, stays there about 3 hours, and returns to 100 percent. What is the best interpretation?
options: A planet crosses in front of the star every 4 days, blocking about 1 percent of its light
The star pulses, becoming 1 percent fainter every 4 days as it expands and contracts
A planet orbits the star every 3 hours
The star moves toward us every 4 days, shifting its spectral lines
Earth's atmosphere gets thicker every 4 days and dims the star
quiz.why: A flat curve with a repeating, sudden dip and return is the signature of a transit. The gap between dips (4 days) is the orbital period; the 3 hours is only how long the crossing takes. Pulsating stars change smoothly, spectral shifts are measured in spectra, not in a light curve, and atmospheric changes would not repeat so regularly.

quiz.q: Astronomers want to detect faint infrared light from some of the earliest galaxies. Which plan best deals with BOTH the absorbing atmosphere AND the infrared glow of warm objects?
options: A 30 m visible-light telescope with adaptive optics on a high mountain
A telescope far from Earth in space, shielded from the Sun and kept very cold
A refracting telescope with a very large lens on a dry mountaintop
A telescope in a room-temperature dome on a mountaintop
A radio dish with a mesh surface in a desert
quiz.why: Most infrared is absorbed by gases in the air, so the telescope should be above it, and warm objects such as Earth and the telescope itself glow in infrared, so it must stay cold, as JWST does with its sunshield. A mountain still has some air, and a warm dome would add glow. Adaptive optics does not stop absorption, and a radio dish detects the wrong wavelengths.

quiz.q: Astronomers want to focus X-rays from gas falling toward a black hole. Which description matches a workable telescope?
options: One large flat mirror hit head-on, on a very high mountain
A large mesh dish like a radio telescope, in a dry desert
Several nested mirror shells hit at a very shallow angle, in orbit above the atmosphere
A large glass lens in orbit, since lenses bend X-rays strongly
Many 8 m visible-light mirrors linked together on Maunakea
quiz.why: X-rays are blocked by the atmosphere, so the telescope must be in space, and X-rays go straight into an ordinary mirror, so grazing-incidence nested mirrors that deflect them gradually are used. A mesh dish suits long radio waves, glass lenses let X-rays pass straight through, and mountain telescopes cannot receive X-rays at all.

quiz.q: Two identical 10 m radio dishes are used together as an interferometer with 100 m between them, at one wavelength. Compared with a single 10 m dish, which statement is correct?
options: The resolution is like a 20 m dish and the light collected is 4 times as much
The resolution is like a 100 m dish and the light collected is 100 times as much
The resolution is the same, but the light collected is 2 times as much
The resolution is like a 100 m dish, but the light collected is only 2 times as much
The resolution is like a 100 m dish, but the light collected is 10 times as much
quiz.why: Interferometry gives the angular resolution of a telescope as wide as the spread of the dishes (about 100 m). The light collected is only the sum of the areas, 2 times that of one dish. A 100 m dish would collect 100 times as much light, but the pair cannot. Adding the diameters (20 m) or scaling light linearly (10 times) are other common mistakes.

quiz.q: An 8 m ground-based telescope (no adaptive optics) and a 2.4 m space telescope both observe in visible light. Which statement compares them correctly?
options: The space telescope collects about 11 times more light because no atmosphere is in the way, and it also shows finer detail
The ground telescope collects more light and also shows finer detail, because its mirror is bigger
The two collect about the same light, but the ground telescope is sharper because of its larger mirror
The space telescope collects more light because it is closer to the stars, but shows the same detail
The ground telescope collects about 11 times more light, but the space telescope shows finer detail
quiz.why: The light-collecting area goes as D², so (8/2.4)² is about 11 times more for the ground telescope. But turbulence blurs ground images to about 0.5 arcsecond, while the space telescope reaches about 0.05 arcsecond. Space is not meaningfully closer to the stars, and the air absorbs little visible light, so it does not give the space telescope more light.
quiz.source: Ch6.2 pt1 slides 2, 5; Ch6.3 slides 5, 9; Cosmic Perspective 6.2-6.3

quiz.q: Astronomers record two spectra of the same galaxy with the same telescope: spectrum A at low spectral resolution and spectrum B at high spectral resolution. Which statement is correct?
options: Spectrum A shows more detail and needs a longer exposure
Spectrum B shows narrow lines that are merged together in A, but it needs a longer exposure
Spectrum B has better angular resolution
Spectrum B can only be recorded from space
Both show the same detail; B is just brighter
quiz.why: Higher spectral resolution separates close lines that merge at low resolution. But it spreads the light out more, so each wavelength gets less of it, and a longer exposure is needed. Spectral resolution is about lines in a spectrum, not about separating objects in the sky, and it does not require space.

quiz.q: A university plans a large new infrared and visible-light telescope. Which site is best?
options: A 500 m hill beside a big city so staff can commute
A calm, dry, high desert plateau far from city lights
A windy sea-level coast, because moving air averages out the blurring
A humid rainforest valley, because water vapour helps infrared light pass
A high mountain inside a large city, for the electricity supply
quiz.why: A good site is calm (less twinkling), dark (little light pollution), high (less air above) and dry (fewer clouds and less water vapour, which absorbs infrared). Wind adds turbulence rather than averaging it out, and city light and low humid air each cause their own problems.

quiz.q: The tiny hole of a pinhole camera (no lens) is made 10 times wider. What happens to the image on the back wall?
options: It becomes dimmer but sharper
It becomes brighter and just as sharp
It becomes dimmer and more blurred
It becomes brighter but more blurred
It is unchanged
quiz.why: A wider hole lets in more light, so the image is brighter. But each point of the object now sends a wider cone of rays through the hole, which lands as a bigger disc on the wall, so the discs overlap and the image blurs. A lens solves both problems by bending the cone back to a single point.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the lens in an eye?
options: to prevent dust and irritants from entering the eye
to bend light entering the eye so that it is focused onto the retina
to adjust the amount of light entering the eye
to send optical signals to the brain to be interpreted
to separate the light collected by the eye into colours
quiz.why: The lens of the eye bends (refracts) incoming light so that it comes to a focus on the retina, where the image is detected. Adjusting how much light enters is the job of the iris and pupil, not the lens. Eyelids, lashes and tears keep out dust, and the retina and optic nerve (not the lens) send the signals to the brain. The eye does not split light into colours.

quiz.q: Which of the following is used in a lens to focus light into an image?
options: Refraction
Transmission
Absorption
Diffraction
Reflection
quiz.why: A lens focuses light by refraction: light changes direction as it passes from air into curved glass, so parallel rays are bent to meet at a focus. Transmission only means light passes through, and absorption removes light instead of focusing it. Reflection is what a mirror uses, not a lens. Diffraction is the spreading of waves at edges, which limits how sharp an image can be but does not form it.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of a longer exposure time when making an image?
options: It allows the detector to collect more total light.
It allows the detector to achieve higher angular resolution.
It allows the detector to measure rapid variations in light intensity.
It allows the detector to record light at very short wavelengths.
quiz.why: A longer exposure lets the detector keep adding up light from a faint source, so it records more total light and can reveal dimmer objects. Angular resolution depends on the telescope's diameter and the wavelength, not on how long you expose. Following rapid changes in brightness needs short exposures, not long ones, and which wavelengths can be recorded depends on the detector itself.

quiz.q: If you want to see the image formed by a telescope, you should place your eye at the location of the telescope's
options: Cassegrain.
focus.
secondary mirror.
primary mirror.
central hole in the primary mirror.
quiz.why: A telescope brings light to a focus, and the image exists at that point, so that is where an eyepiece (or your eye) must be placed to see it. The primary and secondary mirrors only collect and redirect the light. A Cassegrain is a type of telescope design, and the hole in the primary mirror is just a passage the light travels through on its way to the focus.

quiz.q: Which of the following is one important reason why most large astronomical telescopes are reflecting telescopes rather than refracting telescopes?
options: Reflecting telescopes have their heaviest component (the mirror) at the bottom rather than the top of the telescope's tube.
Reflecting telescopes take up less space than refracting telescopes.
Reflecting telescopes are taller than refracting telescopes.
For a mirror and lens of the same diameter, a mirror will collect more light.
quiz.why: A big mirror sits at the bottom of the tube and can be supported across its whole back, while a big lens sits at the top and can be held only around its edge, so it sags under its own weight. That support problem is a major reason why giant telescopes are reflectors. A mirror and a lens of the same diameter collect the same amount of light, so that option is wrong. Reflectors are not taller, and being more compact is a side benefit, not what makes very large telescopes possible.

quiz.q: Which of the following measurements can be made only by recording and comparing the amount of light received from an astronomical source at many different times?
options: the rate at which a variable star brightens and dims
the color of a planet
the general shape of an interstellar cloud of gas
the number of bright stars in a nearby star cluster
quiz.why: To find how fast a variable star brightens and dims you have to measure its brightness again and again and compare the measurements over time. The colour of a planet, the shape of a gas cloud and the number of bright stars in a cluster can all be found from a single image taken at one moment.

quiz.q: Which of the following could not be determined by an observation that only uses spectroscopy?
options: the chemical composition of a distant star
the speed at which a distant galaxy is moving away from us
the surface temperature of a distant star
the rotation rate of a distant star
the angular size of a distant galaxy
quiz.why: A spectrum spreads light out by wavelength, but it is not an image, so it cannot tell you how large an object appears on the sky. Spectral lines still reveal composition (which lines appear), temperature (the shape of the spectrum and which lines are strong), the Doppler shift that gives how fast a galaxy recedes, and rotation (spinning broadens the lines).

quiz.q: What is meant by spectral resolution?
options: It is a measure of how close two stars can be in the sky and still be distinguishable.
It is a measure of how close two spectral lines can be and still be distinguishable.
It is a measure of how much energy an object emits in different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
It is the same as angular resolution but applied to telescopes operating at different wavelengths.
quiz.why: Spectral resolution describes how well a spectrograph can tell two nearby wavelengths apart, meaning how close two spectral lines can be and still be seen as separate lines. How close two stars can be in the sky is angular resolution. Energy emitted at different wavelengths is the spectrum itself, not its resolution, and spectral resolution is not just angular resolution at other wavelengths.

quiz.q: What do astronomers mean by light pollution?
options: Light pollution refers to pollution caused by light industry as opposed to heavy industry.
Light pollution refers to harmful gases emitted by common street lights.
Light pollution refers to light used for human activities that brightens the sky and hinders astronomical observations.
Light pollution refers to the lights that must be used inside major observatories and that make it difficult for astronomers' eyes to adapt to darkness.
Light pollution is another name for sunlight, which makes it impossible to see stars in the daytime.
quiz.why: Light pollution is stray artificial light from cities, streets and buildings that brightens the night sky and washes out faint astronomical objects. It has nothing to do with light industry, harmful gases from lamps or the lights inside an observatory, and sunlight in the daytime is a natural effect, not pollution.

quiz.q: What causes stars to twinkle?
options: The human eye has difficulty seeing faint objects.
Interstellar gas along the line of sight to the star absorbs different amounts of radiation.
Moving gases in Earth's atmosphere randomly bend light rays from stars.
Stars constantly vary in brightness as they expand and contract.
quiz.why: Twinkling happens because pockets of air in Earth's atmosphere are constantly moving, and they randomly bend the starlight in slightly different directions from moment to moment. That makes the star's brightness and position flicker. It is not a weakness of the eye, and stars that are pulsing change over days or longer, not many times a second. Gas between the stars does not flicker on this time scale.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adaptive optics?
options: to increase the collecting area of telescopes on the ground
to reduce the distorting effects of atmospheric turbulence for telescopes on the ground
to allow several small telescopes to work together like a single larger telescope
to increase the magnification of telescopes on the ground
to improve the angular resolution of telescopes in space
quiz.why: Adaptive optics uses a flexible mirror, adjusted many times each second, to cancel the blurring that turbulent air causes, so a ground telescope gets much sharper images. It does not enlarge the collecting area, combine separate telescopes (that is interferometry), or add magnification. Space telescopes are above the air and do not need it.

quiz.q: Which of the following is not a good reason to place an observatory on a remote mountain?
options: allow study of infrared light
reduce the twinkling caused by Earth's atmosphere
reduce the impact of light pollution
allow observations at ultraviolet and x-ray wavelengths
quiz.why: A remote mountaintop helps with infrared light (it is above most of the water vapour that absorbs it), with steadier images (less air above) and with darker skies away from city lights. It does not help with ultraviolet or x-rays, because the atmosphere blocks those wavelengths even at the summit, so they can only be observed from space.

quiz.q: Earth's atmosphere is most transparent to all wavelengths of ________ light.
options: both visible and ultraviolet
ultraviolet
x-ray
visible
infrared
quiz.why: The atmosphere lets visible light through (and radio waves, which are not offered here). Ultraviolet and x-rays are absorbed high in the atmosphere, so options that include them are wrong. Infrared is only partly transmitted: water vapour and carbon dioxide block most of it, leaving a few narrow windows.

quiz.q: What is the best reason to put a visible-light telescope in space instead of on the ground?
options: Space telescopes are not affected by earthquakes.
A space telescope is closer to the source of the light, so it can make a clearer image.
The telescope is above the atmosphere so the light does not get distorted by turbulent air.
It is easier to launch very large space telescopes into space than to find places for them on the ground.
quiz.why: Above the atmosphere there is no turbulent air to blur the light, so a space telescope can reach the sharpness its mirror allows. Being slightly closer to a star changes nothing, since the stars are trillions of kilometres away. Earthquakes are rarely the main problem on the ground, and launching a huge telescope is actually harder than building it on the ground.

quiz.q: The largest diameter telescopes are used to observe
options: infrared light.
x-rays.
ultraviolet light.
visible light.
radio waves.
quiz.why: Radio waves are very long, so a radio telescope must be enormous to reach a useful angular resolution, and radio signals from space are very weak. The surface of a radio dish also only has to be smooth to a fraction of a long wavelength, so huge dishes and arrays are practical. Mirrors for shorter wavelengths have to be polished far more precisely, which limits their size.

quiz.q: Which of the following would be the most useful ultraviolet telescope?
options: a 30-meter telescope on a mountain
a 1-meter telescope in space
a 10-meter telescope on a mountain
a 2.5-meter telescope in space
quiz.why: Ultraviolet light is absorbed by Earth's atmosphere, so a useful ultraviolet telescope has to be in space. That rules out the two mountain telescopes however big they are. Of the two space telescopes, the 2.5-meter one collects about 2.5² ≈ 6 times as much light as the 1-meter one and also has finer resolution.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes how and why x-ray telescopes differ from visible light telescopes?
options: X-ray telescopes use grazing incidence mirrors because x-ray photons will penetrate a normal mirror.
X-ray telescopes have to be built with very thick mirrors because x-ray photons will penetrate a thin mirror.
X-ray telescopes do not use mirrors because x-ray photons cannot be focused.
X-ray telescopes must be much larger because of the small number of x-ray photons.
X-ray telescopes cannot do spectroscopy because all x-ray photons have the same wavelength.
quiz.why: X-ray photons carry so much energy that they would pass into an ordinary mirror instead of bouncing off. They can only be reflected if they skim the surface at a very shallow angle, so x-ray telescopes use nested grazing-incidence mirrors. They can be focused, they do not need thick mirrors, and x-ray photons come in many wavelengths, so spectroscopy is possible.

quiz.q: What does the technique of interferometry allow?
options: It allows two or more telescopes to obtain a total light-collecting area much larger than the total light-collecting area of the individual telescopes.
It allows us to determine the chemical composition of stars.
It allows astronomers to make astronomical observations without interference from light pollution.
It allows the same telescope to make images with both radio waves and visible light.
It allows two or more telescopes to obtain the angular resolution of a single telescope much larger than any of the individual telescopes.
quiz.why: Interferometry combines the signals from several telescopes so that together they achieve the angular resolution of one telescope as wide as the distance between them. It does not create extra light-collecting area (the total light collected is still the sum of the separate telescopes), and it has nothing to do with composition, light pollution or imaging in two kinds of waves.

quiz.q: Astronomers sometimes make use of "neutrino telescopes," which are typically located deep underground. What are neutrinos?
options: a very high-energy form of light
a type of light-weight subatomic particle
a very low-energy form of light
a type of wave predicted to exist by Einstein's general theory of relativity
quiz.why: Neutrinos are extremely light subatomic particles that hardly ever interact with matter, made in nuclear reactions in the Sun and in exploding stars. They are particles, not forms of light of any energy, and they are not the gravitational waves of general relativity. The detectors sit deep underground so that other particles are blocked and only the neutrinos get through.

quiz.q: Are cosmic rays a form of light?
options: No, they consist of high-energy subatomic particles, not of electromagnetic waves.
Yes, they are the name we give to all rays of light that come from the cosmos.
Yes, they are light waves with higher energy than gamma rays.
Yes, they are light waves with lower energy than radio waves.
quiz.why: Cosmic rays are fast-moving subatomic particles, mostly protons and atomic nuclei, not electromagnetic waves, so they are not light. Light of higher energy than gamma rays or lower energy than radio waves does not exist as a separate class, and the name does not mean all light from the cosmos.

quiz.q: What are gravitational waves?
options: the name we give to electromagnetic waves that come from astronomical objects that have gravity
a type of energy that is different from light and that has been detected from sources such as merging neutron stars and black holes
a form of light with higher energy than gamma rays
a form of light with lower energy than radio waves
quiz.why: Gravitational waves are ripples in space and time predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity. They are a different kind of signal from light, and they have been detected from merging black holes and merging neutron stars. They are not electromagnetic waves, so they cannot be light with more energy than gamma rays or less than radio waves.

quiz.q: Which of the following telescopes is best suited for studying the hottest intergalactic gas (10 million K) in a cluster of galaxies?
options: Chandra X-ray Telescope
Very Large Array Radio Telescope
Hubble Space Telescope (UV, optical, and some infrared)
Herschel Infrared Telescope
quiz.why: Gas at 10 million K is so hot that it glows mainly in x-rays, and x-rays are blocked by the atmosphere, so you need an x-ray telescope in space such as Chandra. Radio, ultraviolet/visible and infrared telescopes are suited to cooler material, because hotter objects emit shorter wavelengths.

quiz.q: How does a lens work?
options: It speeds up light traveling through it, delivering more power to the resulting image, which is focused at the focal plane.
It refracts light rays in a manner that renders a coherent image on the image plane.
It reflects light rays in a manner that renders a coherent image at the focal point.
It uses diffraction to separate wavelengths, forming a coherent image on the image plane.
It forces light to travel through a narrow opening, decreasing circles of confusion and resulting in a coherent image on the focal plane.
quiz.why: A lens bends (refracts) light so that rays from each point of the object meet at one point on the image plane, giving a coherent image. Mirrors reflect; a pinhole uses a narrow opening; light actually slows down in glass.

quiz.q: Suppose a 40-meter radio dish is used to observe radio light from a galaxy with a wavelength of 1 meter. Meanwhile, a 10-meter telescope observes infrared light from the same galaxy with a wavelength of 1 micron (10^-6 m). Which statement is true?
options: The radio telescope has 4 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is greater, rendering the radio image less sharp.
The radio telescope has 16 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is smaller, rendering the radio image less sharp.
The radio telescope has 16 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is greater, rendering the radio image less sharp.
The radio telescope has 4 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is smaller, rendering the radio image sharper.
The radio telescope has 16 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is greater, rendering the radio image sharper.
quiz.why: Area grows as D squared: (40/10)^2 = 16 times. Smallest resolvable angle goes as wavelength/D: radio 1/40 = 0.025 versus infrared 10^-6/10 = 10^-7. The radio angle is far larger, so its image is less sharp.

quiz.q: Which of the following steps would NOT help to reduce or eliminate atmospheric distortions that interfere with telescope observations?
options: Putting a telescope in space to bypass the atmosphere.
Waiting for a break in the weather.
Using adaptive optics to account for distortions in real time.
Operating a telescope in a better location with drier air and a higher altitude.
Using interferometry to achieve a better angular resolution across multiple telescopes.
quiz.why: Interferometry links telescopes to act like one very wide dish, improving resolution, but it does nothing about the air bending the light. Space, adaptive optics, high dry sites and clear (calm) skies all reduce what the atmosphere does to the light.

quiz.q: Which of the following wavelength ranges is it best to put a telescope into space to detect?
options: Radio waves
X-rays
Visible
Infrared
None of the above require space telescopes to detect.
quiz.why: The atmosphere absorbs X-rays completely, so X-ray telescopes must be above it. Radio and visible light reach the ground, and much infrared work can be done from high, dry mountains.

order.title: Telescope sizes
order.prompt: Put these light collectors in order of the diameter of their main lens or mirror, from the smallest at the bottom to the largest at the top.
order.why: Your eye's pupil is only a few millimetres wide. Hubble's mirror is 2.4 m, JWST's is 6.5 m, each Very Large Telescope unit is 8.2 m, each Keck telescope is 10 m, and the Extremely Large Telescope will be 39.3 m across. Light-collecting area grows as the square of these numbers.

order.title: Sharpness at different wavelengths
order.prompt: The same size of mirror observes different kinds of light. Order them by the sharpest detail the mirror could resolve, with the coarsest detail at the bottom and the finest at the top.
order.why: The smallest resolvable angle is proportional to wavelength divided by diameter. With the diameter fixed, the longest wavelength (radio) gives the coarsest detail and the shortest (ultraviolet) the finest, which is why a radio telescope must be so much bigger than a visible-light telescope to match it.

order.title: Inside a spectrograph
order.prompt: Put the parts of a spectrograph in the order the light meets them, first at the bottom and last at the top.
order.why: Light from the telescope focus first passes a narrow slit so that only the target's light enters. A collimating mirror makes the rays parallel, a diffraction grating spreads them by wavelength, a camera mirror focuses the spread-out spectrum, and the detector records it.

order.title: Light path in a Cassegrain telescope
order.prompt: Put the journey of starlight through a Cassegrain reflecting telescope in order, first at the bottom and last at the top.
order.why: Starlight enters the open top of the tube and reaches the large primary mirror at the bottom. The primary reflects it up to the smaller secondary mirror, the secondary reflects it back down through the hole in the primary, and a detector or instrument at the focus records it.

layers.name: Secondary mirror reflects it back down
Light passes through the hole in the primary
Detector at the focus records it

sort.title: Ground or space?
sort.prompt: Sort each kind of light or telescope by whether it can work well from the ground or needs space (or a very high flight).
buckets: Needs space or a very high flight

items.text: A few narrow near-infrared bands at a high, dry site
Very Large Array dishes in New Mexico

sort.why: Only visible light, radio waves and a few narrow infrared bands pass through the atmosphere well. Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet and most infrared are absorbed, so they need space or an aircraft high above most of the air.

sort.title: Which technique measures it?
sort.prompt: Sort each question by the main kind of observation that answers it.

items.text: The shape of a spiral galaxy
A star's colour from its B and V brightness
Whether two stars in a cluster are separate points
Which chemical elements a star contains
The speed of a galaxy moving away (Doppler shift)
A star's temperature from its spectrum
The rotation rate of a star from broadened lines
How a Cepheid variable star pulses
Repeating dips as a planet transits
A solar flare brightening and fading
A star's movement across the sky over many years

sort.why: An image records where light comes from and how bright it is in each filter. A spectrum shows intensity at each wavelength, so it reveals composition, temperature, speed and rotation. Time monitoring repeats measurements to see changes in brightness or position.

sort.title: Reflector or refractor?
sort.prompt: Sort each description by the kind of telescope it fits.

items.text: Large main optic held only at its rim
Needs glass that is flawless all the way through
Tube becomes very long for a big telescope
Focuses light with a curved mirror
Main optic supported across its whole back
Only the front surface must be shaped precisely

sort.why: A refractor focuses with a lens, so the glass must be perfect throughout, can be held only at its edge, and splits colours. A reflector focuses with a mirror that is supported from behind, can be built in segments, and has no colour problem, which is why almost every large telescope is a reflector.

sort.title: Light collection or resolution?
sort.prompt: Sort each statement by the property of a telescope it is about.

items.text: Doubling the diameter gives 4 times as much
A longer exposure helps make up for too little of it
Does not depend on the wavelength
For linked telescopes it is just the sum of the individual ones
Depends on wavelength divided by diameter
Doubling the diameter halves the smallest angle
Lets you split a close double star

sort.why: Light-collecting area is about how much light, which goes as D² and just adds up for linked telescopes. Angular resolution is about how fine the detail is, which goes as λ/D, is limited by diffraction and is what interferometry improves.
